query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing minor alloying elements that enhance short-range order (SRO) in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers promotes the formation of diffuse, coherent interfaces that impede dislocation motion and delay the onset of plastic deformation under sustained creep loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale HEA multilayer composed of FCC and BCC phases with conventional alloying and relatively low SRO, exhibiting standard dislocation nucleation and motion.
generation.intervention: Incorporate minor alloying additions designed to increase chemical SRO and thereby promote the formation of more diffuse, coherent interfaces between the layers.
generation.conditions: Subject the multilayers to a sustained creep load under moderate temperatures and stresses that are typical of service conditions, ensuring that the nanoscale coating structure is preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced SRO leading to more diffuse and coherent interfacial structures.
generation.mechanism: The increased SRO stabilizes the interfaces, raising the stress required for dislocation nucleation and mobility; as a result, the progression of dislocation-mediated deformation and the associated phase transformations (e.g., formation of hcp phases via stacking fault processes) are delayed compared to the baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, the SRO-enhanced multilayers will exhibit a lower creep strain rate, a delayed transition from elastic to plastic deformation, and a reduced volume fraction of deformation-induced hcp structures under equivalent loading.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the additional minor alloying elements, which show earlier dislocation activation, higher creep strain rates, and a larger extent of deformation-induced phase transformation.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected as long as the nanoscale multilayer architecture is maintained and the SRO enhancement does not compromise overall ductility; however, at very high temperatures or extreme stresses, thermal activation might overwhelm the stabilizing effects of the enhanced SRO.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of creep rate reduction and the delay in deformation onset are uncertain and will require quantitative experimental calibration, as the interplay between enhanced SRO, interface coherency, and intrinsic lattice distortion in HEAs is complex.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers: one set with the minor alloying elements intended to enhance SRO and one without (control). Subject both sets to identical sustained creep loading tests at moderate temperature and stress. After deformation, compare the creep strain rates, the onset (or delay) of plastic deformation, and microstructural evolution (including phase transitions and interface coherency) using TEM, XRD, and other relevant characterization methods.
measurements: Onset and progression of plastic deformation (yield strain)
Volume fraction of deformation-induced hcp phases
Interface coherency and SRO characterization via microscopy and diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SRO-enhanced multilayers do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate, a delayed onset of plastic deformation, or a reduced fraction of deformation-induced hcp phases relative to the control sample, then the hypothesis—that enhanced SRO through minor alloying improves creep resistance by stabilizing interfaces—is falsified.

In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. This behavior contrasts with the screw dislocation-dominated plasticity typically observed in conventional BCC metals and suggests a distortion-induced shift in the dominant deformation mechanism. The relatively high density of randomly distributed edge segments with multiple slip vectors promotes frequent dislocation interactions and entanglements. These entangled substructures serve as effective barriers that counteract the thermal softening typically observed during single-slip deformation at high temperatures, thereby suppressing strain localization and promoting more uniform deformation. cited_evidence.kind: web:Dislocation mechanisms for fcc to hcp phase transformation
cited_evidence.text: In this process, twin boundaries pose a barrier to dislocations shearing across the interface, while simultaneously redirecting the shear parallel to the interface, thereby forming hcp laths at the twin boundary. In addition, the hcp layers can form by glide of extended dislocations on adjacent planes, which is facilitated by the negative average stacking fault energy of the alloy. The coherent interface between hcp and fcc phases also stops and redirects the incoming dislocations, providing an additional strengthening source. Strong interface barriers such as large angle grain boundaries ordinarily would be expected to cause highly localized stress concentrations at the tips of dislocation pile-ups that could lead to premature crack initiation. Conversely, while the twin/hcp lath structures provides a strong barrier to slip transmission, the redirection of dislocations along the boundary smears out the damaging stress concentrations. With increasing strain, unusually large lattice rotations (greater than 30°) are created within individual grains, which further support the process described.

The expected residual magnitudes for dislocations interacting with the misfit dislocation networks at fcc/bcc interfaces can be rather complicated. We thus attribute a central role to dislocation reactions at the fcc - bcc/B2 interfaces and fcc twin boundaries for the superior work hardening of FeCoCrNiAl0.5. Furthermore, work is needed on effects of composition on the intrinsic energy barriers governing slip and twin and latent- and self- hardening due to twin-twin and twin-slip interactions. The present results evidence twinning in FeCoCrNiAl0.5 both at 77K and room temperature. In contrast, similar experiments on FeCoCrMnNi single crystals found twinning only at 77K,. These observations suggest that replacing Mn by Al leads to a beneficial shift of the nucleation stresses for slip and twin, in favor of twinning at room temperature. Building on this, composition optimization may lead the way to develop novel HEAs with even higher work-hardening.

In our HEAs, the lattice constant and modulus of the ordered L12 precipitates approximate to those of the disordered FCC matrix, and no new FCC−L12 interfaces form after dislocations shear these L12 precipitates with diffuse coherent interfaces. Therefore, strengthening by coherent strain, modulus difference, and interfacial energy increase is negligible. Instead, the L12 nanophases were formed by spinodal decomposition. This spinodal nanostructure can resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating APBs on the slip planes of these ordered L12 nanophases when they are sheared by dislocations. The contribution of the spinodal nanostructure to the YS of 600 A is calculated to be 1158 MPa (see Methods in details). Superposing additional strengthening from grain boundaries and the BCC phases, the total increase in YS is estimated to be 1524 MPa, which agrees with the experimental result of 1536 MPa, confirming that this spinodal order–disorder nanostructure can potently strengthen our alloys. reading.lever: Introduce minor alloying elements to enhance SRO and promote diffuse coherent interfaces in HEA multilayers.
reading.why: This lever builds on evidence that SRO increases dislocation resistance and adjusts interface properties—a mechanism untested in nanoscale multilayer systems.
